{
  "reasoning": "The DUT is a purely combinational two-input block, so its entire input space is four points and exhaustive stimulus is both natural and cheap. Rather than write one broad 'try all four' element per requirement, I split the space so each element pins one distinguishable behaviour and each failure mode has a named home. For REQ-0000 (sum = a XOR b) the four points are separate elements: (0,0) is the all-zeros boundary, (0,1) and (1,0) are the two asymmetric single-operand points -- kept apart deliberately, because a design that ties sum to a single input still passes if only one of the two is driven -- and (1,1) is the corner where the XOR result wraps back to 0 and the carry leaves through cout rather than sum, which is the one point that separates a half adder's sum from an OR. For REQ-0001 (cout = a AND b) the interesting partition is different: (1,1) is the only asserting point and is therefore its own element, (0,0) is the all-zeros boundary, and the two exactly-one-high points share an element because they are the same behaviour and together they are what distinguishes AND from OR. All of these are D1_data_boundary: with one-bit ports every input value is simultaneously a minimum, a maximum and a width edge, so there is no separate 'ordinary' data case to write. One further element is not about data at all: the contract declares is_sequential=false and latency_cycles=0 for both outputs, so the plan carries a D3_timing element that changes the inputs with no clock edge in between and requires both outputs to follow within the same evaluation. That is the element that fails a design which latched or registered its outputs -- a defect the four data points cannot see, because a registered half adder produces exactly the right values one cycle late. Both requirements declare needs=[\"testplan\",\"refmodel\"], so both are legitimately coverable; nothing else in the requirement set is covered, and every reference is pinned at revision 1.",
